correctness.rationale: The precise strict-blocking conditions reduce to all four possible unanimous-better-candidate intersections. Their count inequalities are necessary and sufficient. The finite multinomial distribution follows from six equally likely strict rankings and an at-most-one proof. The full-sequence exponent follows from an exactly normalized likelihood-ratio inequality and matching interior-compatible type construction. On n divisible by six, the tilted multinomial mode bounds all lattice weights; dominated convergence gives the rational sum 14904/121 and Stirling yields the n^-3/2 constant. The standalone checker reproduced 5004 exhaustive ranking-histogram cases and exact probabilities. Computations are not used in place of the analytic infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The primary September 2026 paper defines AWVC and its majority threshold and reports synthetic evaluation, but the inspected mathematical passages do not assert the exact three-alternative top-approval probability, its exponential rate, or its rational lattice prefactor. The older standard proportional veto core has no approval-weighted blocking normalization. Exact same-model comparisons of statements reveal no covering implication, subject to the explicit uninspected-material and unindexed-literature risks.
residual_risks: The 2020/2023 full paper on the classical proportional veto core was not inspected, so an unexpected implication to approval-specific random veto cores cannot be completely ruled out.
The entire 2026 primary paper, especially all supplemental material, was not inspected end-to-end; the sections containing the AWVC definition, guarantees, experiments and algorithm were inspected.
Unindexed, later, or differently named results might contain an equivalent asymptotic; no independence of publication is asserted.

value.rationale: Whether a collective-consent rule can return any permissible alternative is a central motivated question, not an arbitrary invariant. Three strict alternatives form the first natural setting with two distinguishable common-better-veto patterns; single top-choice approvals are the canonical minimal consistent approval input. The theorem provides a structural uniqueness classification, exact finite nonempty probabilities, and a sharp rational lattice prefactor that distinguishes AWVC coalition effects from simple majority approval. It is a nontrivial new typical-case benchmark for the rule despite being restricted to its minimal ordinal domain.
